notes:
I've written up notes on Job 1 below, but some parts are thin. Several page fetches failed or came back cut off, and I couldn't find anything on these sites from Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist, Lutheran or Anglican teachers. Those gaps are listed at the end. On BibleHub and StudyLight several commentators share one page, so I've only named a commentator when the page clearly attributed the remark.

## Job 1 — Research notes

**v. 1**
- Traditional reading: The chapter opens by presenting Job as a deeply righteous man, though not a perfect one. Guzik says "blameless" doesn't mean sinless. He quotes Lawson, who says no one around Job could fairly accuse him of moral failure. enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/ — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- Guzik quotes Andersen: don't play down Job's goodness to fit a doctrine that all people are depraved. Everyone in the book agrees people are sinful, and Job's first act is to offer sacrifices for sin. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- Guzik quotes Morgan: knowing Job was righteous keeps us from thinking his suffering was punishment or correction. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- Guzik quotes Trapp, who says Job was a real person, not a parable, citing Ezekiel 14:14 and James 5:11. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- Piper (Baptist) explains "fearing God" as trembling, wonder, awe and delight in God's presence, together with a fear of dishonouring him. Job's fear of God led him to turn away from evil. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-when-the-righteous-suffer-part-1
- Modern scholarship: Bible Odyssey says Job is not an Israelite but a Gentile from "the land of Uz," perhaps a place in Edom. — https://www.bibleodyssey.org/people/main-articles/job

**vv. 2–3**
- Guzik: in that culture a large family meant high status, and Job's godliness, wealth and standing made him the greatest man in the East. He quotes Mason, who points to later chapters (29:12–17; 31:16–21) showing Job used his wealth to rescue the needy and take in orphans. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/

**v. 4**
- Guzik reads the feasts as a sign of a happy, close family, probably celebrating birthdays, not as wild living. He quotes Andersen: the text gives no hint of drunkenness or laziness. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- Spurgeon (Baptist), quoted by Guzik, argues that if Job had thought the feasting sinful he would simply have forbidden it. Spurgeon took verses 4–5 as permission for believers to celebrate and preached a Christmas sermon on the text. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- A different emphasis: Brown's commentary suggests the children seemed more interested in partying than in staying right with God, so Job felt he had to step in for them. Brown's Commentary — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jbs/job-1.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik sees Job mainly as a careful, godly man acting as priest for his family, not as the father of wicked children. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- One BibleHub commentator says Job reminded his children to examine themselves and confess, and offered for each one as a man hoping for acceptance through the promised Saviour. BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/1-5.htm
- How many offerings? A comment on the same page says it can't be known for sure whether there were ten (one per child) or seven (one per feast day). BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/1-5.htm
- The word "cursed": the Hebrew verb normally means "bless" and is used here as a polite substitute for "curse" (also in 1:11 and 2:5, 9). BibleHub article — https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Job_sacrifice_for_his_children.htm
- Other suggested meanings:
  - Keil and Delitzsch translate it "dismissed God from their hearts." BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/1-5.htm
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown suggest "bid farewell to," taken from the blessing people said when parting. BibleHub — same page
  - Gill takes it in a milder sense: thinking slightingly of God, or giving their own effort the credit for their wealth instead of God's providence. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/job/1-5.html
  - Clarke thinks Job feared his children had slipped into idolatrous thoughts during the feasts, "blessed the gods." StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/job/1-5.html
- Catholic Bible text: Barnes notes the Vulgate oddly renders this "blessed God." BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/1-5.htm
- Pointing to Christ: one BibleHub article says Job's repeated offerings foreshadow Christ's once-for-all sacrifice, and his role as family priest foreshadows Jesus as high priest. BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Job_sacrifice_for_his_children.htm
- Application: Guzik quotes Meyer, who urges parents to keep praying for grown children they can no longer control. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/

**v. 6**
- Most commentators say the "sons of God" are angels (Genesis 6; Job 38:7). Satan coming among them shows he is a created angel, in no way God's equal or opposite. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- The Geneva Bible notes say that although Satan opposes God, he must still obey him and can do nothing without God's permission. BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/1-6.htm
- Barnes quotes Rosenmüller: Satan, like the other heavenly spirits, is under God's rule. BibleHub — same page
- A minority view: Matthew Henry allows that the scene could be an earthly gathering of believers, since godly people in the patriarchal age were called "sons of God." BlueLetterBible — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_001.cfm
- Gill says most interpreters take it as angels but he isn't convinced. He argues that outside this book angels are never called "sons of God." StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/job/1-6.html
- Modern scholarship:
  - Bible Odyssey: in Job the noun has the definite article, "the satan," and should be translated as a title ("the accuser"). This figure is a member of God's court, like a prosecuting attorney, and obeys God. Bible Odyssey — https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/satan/
  - Another Bible Odyssey article goes further and says the accuser is not Satan, the devil, but an angel whose job it is to identify people disloyal to God. — https://www.bibleodyssey.org/people/main-articles/job
  - Barnes reports a similar older view (Herder, Eichhorn and others) that this figure is a faithful but over-suspicious servant of God. He rejects it and calls Satan a malignant being. StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-6.html; https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/job/1-6.html

**v. 7**
- Henry: God knew perfectly well where Satan had been. By asking, he showed that Satan is under his control. BlueLetterBible — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_001.cfm
- Guzik: Satan moves freely about the earth "as a roaring lion" (1 Peter 5:8) and takes an active interest in it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- The Biblical Illustrator reads "going to and fro" as a sign of homelessness and zeal. StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-12.html
- Modern scholarship: Peake observes that the Satan is still something of a free agent, since even God asks where he has been. StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-1.html

**v. 8**
- Guzik: God himself raises Job's name and in effect boasts about him. This verse and the prologue are the only fully objective view of Job in the book; later speakers all have their own biases. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- Guzik quotes Mason: all charges against Job have been dropped by the one he offended. Guzik compares this to believers being fully justified in Christ. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- Henry: God speaks first to get ahead of Satan's accusations. God knows all the malice of the devil, and we have an advocate even before we are accused. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-6.html
- Piper: Job's fear of God put God's worth on display so clearly that God "beamed over" him in front of Satan. desiringgod.org — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-when-the-righteous-suffer-part-1

**v. 9**
- Guzik: here Satan plays "the accuser of the brethren" (Revelation 12:10), claiming Job serves God only for what he gets. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- Constable quotes the line that cynicism is the essence of the satanic: the Satan thinks nothing is genuinely good, neither Job's piety nor God's generosity. StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-21.html
- Henry: it was true that Job didn't fear God for nothing, since godliness is great gain. But it was false that he would stop fearing God without the reward. He also notes the irony: Job's friends charged him with hypocrisy because he was greatly afflicted, Satan because he greatly prospered. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-6.html
- Modern scholarship: Bible Odyssey states the book's question this way: are people righteous only for what they can get out of such behavior? — https://www.bibleodyssey.org/people/main-articles/job

**v. 10 — the "hedge"**
- Gill describes the hedge as God's love, power, providence and angels around Job, so strong that neither men nor devils could break through. StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-10.html
- Henry: God's people are under his special protection, both their spiritual lives and their everyday lives. BlueLetterBible — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_001.cfm
- Guzik compares it to Jesus' words to Peter in Luke 22:31–32 about a similar hedge of protection. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- Applied to believers today:
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) sees the hedge as God's protection around his children, citing Psalm 91. StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-6.html
  - J. Vernon McGee: "I believe that there's a hedge about every believer today." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-12.html
- Coffman takes the verse as proof that serving God is usually rewarded in this life too. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-6.html
- Modern scholarship: Peake compares the hedge to the one around a valuable vineyard (Isaiah 5:5). StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-1.html
- Bible Odyssey: the satan charges Job with a piety propped up by too many material blessings, acting more like God's prosecuting attorney than God's divine adversary. — https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/legal-language-in-job/

**v. 11**
- Henry suggests Satan's "surely" hides an unspoken oath, something like "let me perish if he doesn't curse you." StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-6.html
- The Pulpit Commentary notes Satan says Job will curse God, but the outcome is that Job openly blesses him. The same Hebrew word is used in both opposite senses, which sharpens the contrast. BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/1-21.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: God gave Satan wide but limited permission. He lowered the hedge without removing it entirely. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- Barnes notes that the permission included Job's sons and daughters as well as his property. StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-12.html
- Gill explains that Satan left the place where God met with his worshippers. He did not leave God's presence everywhere, since that is impossible. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-12.html
- Coffman says that, according to 1 Corinthians 10, Satan can't tempt even the weakest believer beyond what they can bear. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-9.html
- Coffman also argues that because humanity chose to serve Satan, his request to afflict Job was in a sense within his rights as mankind's chosen ruler. StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-6.html

**vv. 13–19**
- Guzik: with his new freedom Satan did as much damage as he could, cramming the whole disaster into a few hours. Job lost his oxen, servants, sheep, camels and children. enduringword.com — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- On the "fire of God" (v. 16), Spurgeon thinks Satan wanted Job to believe God had turned against him. It failed: seeing God's hand actually took the sting out of the blow. StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-21.html
- Modern scholarship: Peake notes that Satan's work is shown while he himself stays out of sight. He quotes a description of the gap between verses 12 and 13 as an ominous silence before the storm: the reader knows what is coming, Job doesn't. StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-1.html

**v. 20**
- Guzik's summary: instead of cursing God, Job worships him and admits everything came from the Lord and was the Lord's to take. enduringword.com — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- Piper is struck that Job tears his robe, shaves his head and weeps, yet still says "God did it" and worships. desiringgod.org — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-when-the-righteous-suffer-part-1

**v. 21 — where Protestant teachers differ most**
- Common ground:
  - Job came into the world with nothing, so everything he had was a gift, and his wealth came from God's blessing, not luck or skill. enduringword.com — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
  - Henry: Job looks past the human and natural causes to the first cause. He doesn't say "the Sabeans took it" or "the devil made me poor." StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-21.html
  - Gill: the raiders, fire and wind were Satan's tools, and Satan had no power except what God gave him. Gill limits the verse to earthly things, because God's spiritual gifts are never taken back (Romans 11:29). BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/1-21.htm
- Reformed and Baptist emphasis:
  - Piper heads one point "Satan's work is ultimately the work of God". — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-reverent-in-suffering
  - Elsewhere he says Job's answer to "who killed the kids?" is God, and that saying so was not sin. desiringgod.org — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-when-the-righteous-suffer-part-1
  - H.B. Charles Jr. (Baptist): Job did not say the Lord gave but Satan took away; God alone provided and withdrew Job's blessings. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/charles_hb/articles/devotional/the-test-of-true-worship.cfm
  - Barnes: the loss was no accident but the work of intelligent design, whoever the immediate agent was. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-21.html
- A softer evangelical emphasis: GotQuestions says that, despite this verse, Scripture doesn't teach that God is the author of suffering. In Job's case Satan was behind the tragedies, masterminding the pain, and God allows suffering and uses it for good. — https://www.gotquestions.org/the-Lord-gives-and-the-Lord-takes-away.html
- Guzik (Calvary Chapel) takes a middle line: Job was right that God was ultimately behind everything, even if the immediate responsibility for an event was not God's. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- Translation note: GotQuestions points out that some versions make this a statement about Job's case ("gave… has taken away," ESV), others a general truth ("gives… takes away," NET). GotQuestions — same page
- Prosperity teaching, as reported by a critic: H.B. Charles says prosperity preachers claim Job made his situation worse by speaking a negative confession; God only gives and never takes away. He answers with verse 22. Note this is his account of their view; I didn't find a source from that movement itself. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/charles_hb/articles/devotional/the-test-of-true-worship.cfm
- Worship: Desiring God says worshipping in trial declares God more valuable than anything he gives. desiringgod.org — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-lord-gave-and-took-away
- Spurgeon: Job means God is to be blessed both for giving and for taking. StudyLight — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/1-21.html
- Catholic and Greek Bible texts: the Septuagint and the Vulgate (Douay-Rheims) add "as it pleased the Lord, so is it done." BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/niv/job/1-21.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: "the name of Jehovah" here suggests the name was known in Uz but rarely used. BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/1-21.htm

**v. 22**
- Guzik: this verse shows Job did not sin when he said "the LORD has taken away." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/
- Piper agrees that what Job said was not sin. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-when-the-righteous-suffer-part-1
- H.B. Charles: it isn't wrong to say the Lord gave and took away. It is wrong to receive blessings from the Lord and refuse to receive trouble. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/charles_hb/articles/devotional/the-test-of-true-worship.cfm
- GotQuestions: Job didn't understand why God allowed it but accepted that he didn't understand everything. — https://www.gotquestions.org/the-Lord-gives-and-the-Lord-takes-away.html
- Modern scholarship: Bible Odyssey notes that the prose frame shows a "patient" Job, but in the rest of the book Job is an outspoken rebel. — https://www.bibleodyssey.org/people/main-articles/job

---

**Gaps:**
- I found no Catholic or Orthodox commentary from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. The only Catholic material is the Vulgate/Douay wording noted at vv. 5 and 21.
- I found nothing from named Methodist (Wesley), Lutheran or Anglican teachers.
- I didn't get NET Bible notes, Ellicott, or the Pulpit Commentary on vv. 1–4 and 13–20.
- The Enduring Word page cut off partway through v. 9. Its notes on vv. 20–22 come from a search excerpt, so I don't have Guzik's comments on vv. 10–19 beyond those excerpts.
- The prosperity-teaching view is only reported second-hand by a critic.
